name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a family farm, 110 hectares of barley and wheat and two sheds where we finish about 1,200 pigs a year. My grandfather bought the first fields, my father Walter still lives in the old house across the yard, and I run it now. I'm in the pig sheds at six, checking water, feed and any sick ones, then it's the grain or repairs till dark. My wife Anna does the books by hand in a ledger, the way my mother did, and she works mornings at the church school office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value most about the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That it's ours, and that it's honest. You feed the pigs, you sow the barley, and what you get is what you earned. My son Jonas is fourteen and already drives the old tractor in the yard, and Greta, who's ten, names every runt in the shed. I don't use the computer things, and I don't see why I'd start. We took a loan for the new pig shed four years ago, and that's the one thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I could have told them that for free. Every few years there's a new thing that's going to change farming, and the pigs still need feeding at six. At church on Sunday I'd say the same, and most of the older men would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, so my worries are the old ones. Pig prices go up and down like the weather. When pig prices are down, we lose money on every pig that leaves the yard. The shed loan has six years left, and two bad years in a row would hurt us badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming exactly as we do. If pig prices dropped, I'd stop buying new tools and put off fixing the barn roof. Anna would trim the house budget, like she always does, without being asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the same as every year. You never fully relax on a pig farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said two bad years would hurt. What would that look like for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use up the savings, about four months' worth, then ask the bank for a break on the shed loan. Father would offer money from his pension, and I'd hate to take it. I'd sooner sell some of the barley land than take money from him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame when pig prices drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly the big processors, who set the price and take their cut whatever happens. Partly the rules, all the forms and inspections that cost money and never sell a pig. But mostly it's just the market, and you ride it out like your father did.

say: I could have told them **for free** that the hype wouldn't last.
The **pigs still need feeding** at six, whatever the newest thing is.
think: My worries are old ones: **pig prices** going up and down.
The **shed loan** has six years left, and two bad years would hurt badly.
do: Keep farming **exactly as we do**, with no new tools.
Put off fixing the **barn roof** if pig prices drop.
Let Anna **trim the house budget**, as she always does.
feel: **Uneasy**, as every year on a pig farm.
S0.quote: When pig prices are down, we lose money on every pig that leaves the yard.
fieldNote: Karl's worries are the **pig price cycle** and the shed loan, not AI.
He'd rather **sell land** than take his father's pension money.
He blames **processors and rules**, but mostly accepts the market.
He is **proud** of a hard, honest, hands-on living.

steps.text: Keep finishing 1,200 pigs a year the same way
Put off the barn roof repair if pig prices fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for offices, not farms. The pig processor will answer the phone with a machine and plan the lorries with a machine, and that's their business. I'd tell the men at church that a pig doesn't care how clever the office is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it touches me much. The thinking side of my farm is Anna's ledger and a few phone calls, and she won't swap her ledger for a computer any more than I will. If robots come slowly, I'll be retired before they're any good in a pig shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep the farm running the way it runs. If the processor makes everything online, I'd ask Jonas to do it, because he's good with phones, or I'd ring and insist on talking to a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about me, more that the world's moving and I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be retired before robots are good in a pig shed. When were you planning to retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty-five, maybe later, like my father. So that's 2048. If robots are slow, I don't see a robot that can lift a sick pig and know what's wrong with it before I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the processor started paying more to farms that use their AI planning system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be cross, and I'd still think about it for a long time. I'd probably let Jonas set it up and keep an eye on it. But I'd want to see what it costs and who sees our numbers first.

say: This change is for **offices, not farms**, like the processor's phones and lorries.
A pig doesn't care **how clever** the office is, so the sheds carry on.
think: The thinking side of my farm is **Anna's ledger** and a few phone calls.
If robots come slowly, I'll be **retired** before they're good in a pig shed.
do: Keep the farm running **the way it runs** now.
Ask **Jonas** to handle any online system the processor brings in.
Insist on **talking to a person** when I ring the processor.
feel: **A bit uneasy**, because the world's moving and I'm not.
S1.quote: I don't see a robot that can lift a sick pig and know what's wrong with it before I retire.
fieldNote: Karl sees Steady Disruption as **someone else's problem**, aimed at offices.
He expects to **retire before robots** matter in his sheds.
He leans on **his son Jonas** for anything digital, without learning it himself.
His unease is about **being left behind**, not about losing income.

steps.text: Keep running the pig sheds and grain as now
Wait and see before joining any processor AI scheme
Have Jonas handle the processor's online system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have been fools to let a few companies change everything this fast. I'd say it at church and at the market, and I wouldn't be polite about it. Families and farms should come before what some company in the city wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know what I'd do, and that frightens me more than I'd say. By 2031 the big pig units will have robots and no wages to pay, and they'll sell pork for less than it costs me to grow it. I've no plan for that, and I'm not built to come up with one quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every bit of spending on the farm that isn't feed or the loan. I'd put whatever we could aside, maybe 300 a month, and pay the shed loan down faster. And I'd sit down with my father and Anna and work out what the family could do together, maybe renting out land or Anna taking more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Lying awake at three, listening to the pigs, wondering how long they're mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots around 2031. Does that gap give you any room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but not much use to me. The office side is Anna's ledger, so 2028 changes almost nothing here, and then in 2031 everything changes at once. Three years isn't long enough for a man like me to learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd talk to your father and Anna first. Would you ask anyone outside the family for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pastor, maybe, and the other farmers at church. We've helped each other through floods and fires, so we'd help each other through this. I'd not want government money, but I'd take help from people I know.

say: People were **fools** to let a few companies change everything this fast.
**Families and farms** should come before what city companies want.
think: I **don't know** what I'd do, and that frightens me.
By 2031 **robot pig units** could sell pork below my costs.
do: Stop all farm spending except **feed and the loan**.
Save about **300 a month** and pay the shed loan down faster.
Plan with **my father and Anna**, maybe renting out land.
feel: **Sick and sleepless**, wondering how long the pigs are mine.
S2.quote: By 2031 the big pig units will have robots and no wages to pay, and they'll sell pork for less than it costs me to grow it.
fieldNote: Karl has **no plan** and admits he isn't built to make one quickly.
He'd turn to **family and church**, not government help.
The gap before robots barely helps, since his **thinking work** is tiny.
He blames **a few companies** for letting change come this fast.

steps.text: Stop all farm spending except feed and the shed loan
Save about 300 a month and overpay the shed loan
Plan with Walter and Anna about renting out some land
Ask the pastor and church farmers for help through it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better use these years well, because they won't come again. At church I'd say families should talk now about what the young ones will do. I'd still say nobody voted for any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the pig sheds would be finished by about 2034, maybe sooner. But the shed loan would be paid off by then, and the land is ours, so we'd still have something. I'd be 51, and that's old to start over but not too old to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two first, to see if it was really coming, because I've heard big promises before. I'd keep paying extra off the shed loan so it's clear by 2030. And I'd tell Jonas to do an apprenticeship as an agricultural mechanic, because somebody has to fix those robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not in a panic. More like a long winter you can see coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell Jonas to fix robots, but you'd never use one yourself. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. It's my son learning the thing I won't. But a father's job is to make sure his son can earn a living, not to make him live in the past with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your father, Walter, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would be 82 in 2034, and he'd stay in the old house whatever happens. That's not up for discussion. If we rent the land out, he still gets to walk the fields every morning.

say: We'd better **use these years** well, because they won't come again.
Families should talk now about what **the young ones** will do, and nobody voted for this.
think: The **pig sheds** would be finished by about 2034.
The loan would be paid and **the land is ours**, so we'd still have something.
do: **Wait** a year or two to see if it's really coming.
Overpay the **shed loan** so it's clear by 2030.
Steer Jonas toward an **agricultural mechanic** apprenticeship.
feel: **Worried**, like a long winter you can see coming.
S3.quote: A father's job is to make sure his son can earn a living, not to make him live in the past with me.
fieldNote: Karl admits a **contradiction**: his son learns the robots he refuses.
Owning **land outright** gives him some floor to stand on.
He'd still **wait first**, true to his habit.
His father's place on the farm is **not negotiable**.

steps.text: Wait a year or two before changing anything
Overpay the shed loan so it's clear by 2030
Steer Jonas into an agricultural mechanic apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change in between. Plenty of experts were wrong before. I'd tell people not to sell their land on the strength of a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be all right. By 2039 I'd be 56, the shed loan long paid, and Jonas would be 27 and could run the place with machines if that's how it goes. I'd keep working the parts the robots can't, and the land stays in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing. I'd keep farming the way we farm. Over the years I'd want Jonas to train as a mechanic and then come home, so the farm passes on with someone who knows the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A bit sad, maybe, that it won't look like my father's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd be all right. What could go wrong in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pig prices, same as ever. And if Jonas doesn't want the farm, the whole plan falls apart. I've not actually asked my son Jonas if he wants the farm, and I suppose I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm afraid of the answer, probably. Anna says I should, and Anna's usually right. I'd ask Jonas at harvest, when we're in the tractor together and he can't escape.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and plenty can change.
People shouldn't **sell their land** on the strength of a prediction.
think: I think we'd be **all right**, with the loan long paid by 2039.
**Jonas** could run the place with machines when he's 27.
do: Plan for Jonas to **train as a mechanic** and then come home.
Ask Jonas **at harvest** whether he even wants the farm.
feel: **Fairly settled**, a bit sad it won't look like my father's farm.
S4.quote: I've not actually asked my son Jonas if he wants the farm, and I suppose I should.
fieldNote: Karl's calm rests on a **plan for his son** he hasn't checked with him.
He admits he's **afraid of the answer**, which is honest and revealing.
Owning the land and clearing the loan make **ten years** feel safe.
Pig prices remain the **old worry** in the background.

steps.text: Keep farming the pigs and grain as now
Ask Jonas at harvest whether he wants to take on the farm
Plan for Jonas to train as a mechanic and come home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything but watch. What would help is people I know, our church and the other families, standing together, and the government keeping out of the way with its forms. And maybe somebody to tell farmers like me plainly what's coming, without selling me anything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the old people. My father has lived on this farm for 74 years, and nobody seems to think about what a man like that does when a machine does the work he knows.

headlineQuote: My father has lived on this farm for 74 years, and nobody seems to think about what a man like that does when a machine does the work he knows.
portrait: Karl Bauer is a 43-year-old **pig and grain farmer** on land his grandfather bought.
He **never uses AI** and leaves anything digital to his son Jonas.
His steady worries are **pig prices** and the loan on the new pig shed.
Fast AGI leaves him with **no plan**, turning to family and church.
With more time he pins his hopes on **Jonas taking over**, though he hasn't asked him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to do anything but watch.
whatWouldHelp: **Church and families** standing together, and the government keeping its forms away.
Someone to tell farmers **plainly** what's coming, without selling anything.
